title: Ad-Hoc Runtime Rule/Policy Engine
pattern: Defining business logic as dynamic data rows (containing strings representing fields, values, and actions) evaluated sequentially by a loop.
why_bad: It breaks cohesion by scattering business policies across database records and uncompiled code. The execution order of rules can cause silent side effects or circular dependency loops, and any change to logic bypasses compilation type safety.
detection: A collection of rules loaded from files or database tables at runtime, evaluated dynamically inside an iterative loop that performs string matching on field names.
counterexample: `Context-dependent`. If business logic is modified daily by end-users or operations staff who cannot deploy new binaries, an externalized, sandboxed rules engine is necessary.
source: Eric Evans - _Domain-Driven Design - Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software_ (2003, Addison Wesley).pdf, Chapter 9 "Specifying with Rules" & Chapter 10 "Rules Engines".
